newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-VOLVO CARS DRIVE FIRST QUARTER PROFITS UP.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VOLVO CARS DRIVE FIRST QUARTER PROFITS UP.

text.p: Volvo's car business drove the Swedish vehicle maker to a better-than-expected result in the first quarter of 1997 and analysts said on Wednesday that full-year forecasts would rise.

AB Volvo's operating profit accelerated 60 percent to 1.89 billion crowns ($247 million) to March 31. The increase was led by its cars division where operating profit was 1.07 billion crowns after a loss of 191 million crowns in the same period a year ago.
The operating profit included a 200 million crowns boost from currency movements and 63 million crowns from recently bought units.
"This was a very good report, particularly on the car side," analyst Philip Ayton from BZW told Reuters.
"Volvo had a very good fourth quarter last year but it was not clear if this was a one-off or a new trend. It now appears to be a new trend and will have some impact on the full year."
The market welcomed the result and Volvo's share price climbed 9.5 crowns to 203 crowns in morning trade.
Volvo's first quarter sales rose to 41.85 billion crowns from 39.07 billion a year earlier, pumped up by car sales that rose 18 percent to 23.07 billion crowns.
The number of cars invoiced rose to 94,500 from 85,200.
"It does not seem that Volvo has joined in the price war in the U.S.," analyst Karl-Johan Bonnevier from Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said.
"The change from the 400 series to the S40/V40 models has also been successful in helping margins up."
The improvement was especially noticeable in Europe with the company lifting market share to 1.8 from 1.3 percent.

Volvo's truck sales fell six percent to 10.94 billion crowns while the unit's operating profit fell to 304 million crowns from 731 million crowns in 1996, hit by smaller margins and volumes of sales in Europe.
The problems in this division have been known in the market for nearly a year and were factored into the market view of Volvo. Analysts said the truck results were as expected.
"Volvo Truck is still being charged with losses in the North American operations," outgoing chief executive Soren Gyll said in a statement.
"Vigorous measures are underway to restore the profitability of the U.S. business. Volvo Trucks' profits in Europe continue to be good."
Volvo's pre-tax profit soared to 5.25 billion crowns from 1.92 billion crowns which was above market expectations of 5.10 billion crowns.
However this sum included a capital gain of 3.03 billion crowns from the sale of shares in drinks group Pripps Ringnes to Orkla , the Norwegian company.

The sale was part of Volvo's strategy to sell off non-core assets to concentrate on its main businesses. This is now nearing completion with only a shareholding in drugs company Pharmacia & Upjohn to be sold.

"Developments during the first three months of the year represent the continuation of a positive trend that began in the autumn of 1996," said Gyll. He is to be replaced by Leif Johansson, head of appliance maker Electrolux .
